name: PT Indo Boga Sukses Tbk

frontmatter.title: A property estate holding a stake in the fish trade
frontmatter.summary: Indo Boga Sukses moved its fish-trading assets into a large investment line at 30 June 2026, so the group the market prices as a fish trader is now a restaurant, banqueting and hotel estate carrying a property base built for a business it no longer owns. The estate earns little after depreciation, the investment credit is a house judgement, and the shares price a path the filings do not show.
thesis: The perimeter broke on 30 June 2026: the new investment line of IDR162.5bn equals the operating assets that left the balance sheet (inventory, construction in progress and other assets), so the fish trading book stops contributing revenue from the second half [S5].

What remains is an estate carrying a property base built for the old business: depreciation of IDR5.3bn in a single half year against a full-year revenue path that is a fraction of the group it used to be [S5, S4].

The transfer created the group's largest asset with no ownership percentage, no equity-accounted earnings and no impairment test; we credit it at a discount that is a house judgement, not a sourced value, and the valuation is sensitive to it [S5, S4].
Earnings quality has not improved with the perimeter: operating cash flow was IDR-1.3bn in FY2025A against reported profit of IDR2.1bn, and the divergence runs back through the pack [S4, S0].
At Rp72 against our target of Rp14 the shares discount a revenue path the reverse DCF cannot even bracket, on a balance sheet whose largest asset is unexplained [S0].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results, the first full-year test of whether the fish book still consolidates and whether the investment line carries earnings
Any disclosure on the three investees named in the first-half investment note, or an impairment of that balance
Segafredo Caffe rollout beyond the Yogyakarta flagship, with franchise fee and capex disclosure

blocks.text: **SELL**, target Rp14 against a last price of Rp72: a total return of -80.5% [S0]. The target is built in two steps that run in parallel, not one on top of the other. The valuation is a single discounted cash flow, which values the estate's forecast cash flows, adds the investment line in the bridge and divides by the shares, giving Rp12; there is no method blend, because no multiple can be put on the same perimeter (the valuation section sets out why). Separately, the same model is re-run under each of the three scenarios, with base at 50.0%, bear at 25.0% and bull at 25.0%, and those three values are weighted to Rp16 before the liquidity discount of 10.0% we apply for a stock that turns over IDR1.3bn a day [S0]. The Rp14 target is that scenario-weighted figure after the discount. The scenario weighting is applied once, to the three runs of the one method.

PT Indo Boga Sukses Tbk is a micro-cap on the Indonesia Stock Exchange that the market still reads as a fish trader wearing a restaurant balance sheet. The filings describe the reverse since 30 June 2026. In the six months to that date the fish book was IDR45.1bn of IDR52.5bn of revenue on cost of revenue of IDR40.3bn [S5]. At the period end the balance sheet carries a new investment line of IDR162.5bn in three named entities, against nil at the prior year end, and the assets that funded it left the operating group: inventory fell from IDR69.5bn to IDR8.6bn, fixed assets to IDR189.0bn, and other assets by a similar order [S5 note 14]. The falls and the new line offset almost exactly, which is what a loss of control looks like in the accounts. From 1 July the group earns the restaurant, banqueting and hotel estate and owns a stake in the business that used to be its revenue.

The variant view is not that the company is small or that the estate is worthless. It is that the equity is priced for two things the filings do not support: fish revenue that the group no longer consolidates, and an investment balance whose worth nobody has disclosed. On our numbers the estate generates revenue of IDR15.9bn in the first full year after the transfer, on which it earns IDR-1.4bn of EBIT because the gross profit it keeps after depreciation has to carry a cash operating cost larger than the residue [S5, S4]. The discounted cash flow values the whole equity at Rp12 a share and almost all of that is the credit on the investment line; on the estate's own cash flows, after the two working-capital reversals and the net debt dated to the half year, the operating business is worth a small fraction of the credit. Both are far below Rp72.

Three things move the value. First, the investment credit: we carry the line at seventy per cent of book for the valuation haircut and at a one-in-four chance of a total write-down, so the expected value of the line is just over half of book, and net of the two working-capital reversals and the net-debt dating it covers only a small part of the distance between our target and the price [S5]. Second, the estate path: the gross margin is now the measured estate margin, so the swing is outlet count and banqueting volume rather than a fish spread. Third, what the price is paying for: at 1.7x book and 40.1x trailing EBITDA, the shares need a re-rating to a business the accounts do not describe [S0].

Indonesian small-cap consumer names often carry a premium because the local investor base prices a brand and a property portfolio rather than a cash-flow stream. That habit is what the multiple-survival test exists to police, and it is why an owner of the asset should not pay for earnings that are not there.
The company runs three things, and the weight between them changed at 30 June 2026 [S5].

**The investment line.** The largest asset on the balance sheet and the least disclosed. At 30 June 2026 the group reports IDR162.5bn of investments in PT Javaindo Maju Sejahtera, PT Indo Nation Harvest and a third entity named in the note, against nil at 31 December 2025 [S5 note 14]. There is no ownership percentage, no share of profit, no fair-value exercise and no impairment test on the balance. The entities are the natural home of the fish business the group ran until the half year: PT Indo Nation Harvest is described in the same filing as a trading company [S5 note 1d]. The group now holds a stake in the trade rather than the trade itself.

**Food and beverage.** Restaurants, banqueting and events, and after the transfer the majority of group revenue. FY2025A revenue was IDR8.7bn [S6] and the first half of 2026 printed IDR4.7bn on food cost of IDR1.2bn [S5], a food margin far above the fish book. The estate includes a banqueting venue with a seated capacity of 2,000 people, a timber-built bar and kitchen concept, and a lounge [S6]. This is where the margin lives: the segment earned roughly three-quarters of a rupiah of gross profit per rupiah of revenue in the half year, and that is the margin the model now carries.

**Rooms.** A hotel asset with occupancy of 70.0% [S6], revenue of IDR2.2bn in FY2025A and IDR1.2bn in the first half of 2026 [S6, S5]. Small, stable, and a larger share of the group only because the group is smaller.

**The growth story the company is selling.** IBOS holds the exclusive franchise development rights for Segafredo Caffe in Indonesia under an exclusive franchise development agreement, and has opened a flagship outlet in Sleman, Yogyakarta, which began serving customers at the end of October 2026 and was formally opened in early November 2026 [S9]. The president director calls the outlet a first step and sets out a plan of flagship cafes and kiosks in strategic locations including transport hubs [S9]. The annual report had already set out the pipeline: outlets at the international departures terminal at Soekarno-Hatta, the departures terminal at Yogyakarta International Airport and at Ngurah Rai in Bali, a flagship in Yogyakarta, and a canned sparkling drink under a separate brand through a subsidiary [S6]. That is a credible consumer franchise opportunity and the one part of the equity a bull can legitimately point to. The valuation question is pacing and capital: it is a rollout of individual outlets funded by a company with negative operating cash flow, and the first one is now open.

**Footprint and scale.** The company employed 38 people at the end of 2025 [S6]. That is the most useful number in the annual report for calibrating what this business is: a quoted company with a property portfolio, an investment in a trading book and a franchise licence, run by a few dozen people. It supports the view that the restaurant estate is largely subcontracted or franchised in substance, and it caps how fast a rollout can be executed without a step change in operating cost.

**Ownership and control.** PT Goldman Investindo Sedaya held 61.5% of the shares on the market data, and the interim filing shows the same vehicle with a direct holding of just under half the register [S0, S5]. The free float is 36.0% [S0]. The board is chaired by Nita Fredrika as president commissioner, with Edi Nugroho as president director [S6]. Control is concentrated, the float is small, and the related-party links described in the governance section run through the controlling vehicle.
Two industries now, and the company is a participant in one and a shareholder in the other [S5, S6].

**The estate industry.** Indonesian food and beverage manufacturing grew 7 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 on the statistics agency measure, alongside national growth of a similar order that quarter [S7]. Demand is not the problem. The industry is large, growing and structurally attractive to branded operators, and the categories IBOS is licensed in, Italian coffee and casual dining, are where Indonesian urban demand has been compounding. The estate is a regional operator in that market: a banqueting venue, a small hotel and a coffee franchise, not a national chain.

**Fish trading, now at one remove.** Indonesia is a large fish producer, and the trading layer between landing and end-user is competitive, fragmented and price-transparent: both sides quote against daily market prices, working capital is inventory, and the trader earns a spread that compresses whenever supply is heavy or a supplier gains leverage. That is the business the group has just placed inside three investees. The disclosed evidence on the spread is the half year: fish revenue of IDR45.1bn against cost of revenue of IDR40.3bn, a margin in the low teens [S5]. The group now earns whatever share of that spread the investees distribute, and the filing does not say what share that is.

**The drivers in our sector deck** reach the remaining estate only indirectly. It prices no palm product, so the deck cooking-oil series is not its input. Its input is flour and pastry for the restaurants and banqueting kitchen, which is why the model links cost of revenue to the agriculture deck wheat series at US$294/t US dollars a tonne [S6]. The soymeal link is kept at a minimal weight because the fish-feed channel left the perimeter with the trading book; what remains is fish bought at retail for menus, priced off the deck feed proxy at US$411/t US dollars a tonne [S6]. We hold both exposures small: a large deck link would double-count what the gross-margin line already carries.

**Regulation.** Nothing in the filings points to a licence or tariff that gates the estate. The relevant matters are ordinary: food-safety and halal certification, and the tax treatment of a small profit base, which carried an effective rate above statutory in FY2025A on non-deductible items and none at all in the first half of 2026 [S4, S5]. Franchise development also carries the usual royalty and outlet-approval obligations to the brand owner, which sit inside the franchise agreement rather than in public filings [S9].

**Market share and position.** Challenger, not leader. In the estate it is a regional operator with a handful of venues and a newly acquired national franchise licence; the licence is genuinely differentiated because it is exclusive, but one open outlet is not yet a position. In the fish trade it is now a minority holder in a price-taking business. The five-forces read on the estate is mixed: buyer power is high in banqueting and dining because customers can go elsewhere, supplier power is low in food inputs, and barriers to entry are low for a restaurant but real for the brand licence. The force that works in the company favour is the exclusivity of the Segafredo development right [S9].

**External influences.** Currency matters less than it did: with the trading book outside the perimeter, the estate dollar exposure is the imported content of flour and equipment, not a commodity book. The deck rupiah assumption for next year is Rp18,350/USD rupiah to the dollar [S0]. Rates matter because the company carries bank debt of IDR17.5bn with no disclosed headroom [S5]. Neither is the swing factor. The swing factor is estate volume and the investment balance.

**Revenue.** Group revenue fell from IDR81.0bn in FY2022A to IDR42.8bn in FY2025A, with the sharpest step in FY2024A [S0, S4]. That step was not the fish book: food and beverage revenue fell from IDR20.7bn in FY2023A to IDR8.7bn in FY2025A while fish trade was flat, down a fraction of one per cent in FY2024A [S8 note 26, S6 p.86]. The first half of 2026 reset the level again, with revenue of IDR52.5bn, almost all of it fish at IDR45.1bn [S5]. Our forecast then follows the perimeter. FY2026E of IDR59.8bn is the half-year actual plus a second half carrying only the estate at the level it printed in the first; FY2027E of IDR15.9bn is the first full estate year, the half-year estate level annualised and grown. The -73.5% step between the two years is the transfer leaving the consolidation, not an organic decline, and it is the single most important line in the model: it is why the revenue base is a fraction of what the market still sees in the trailing figures. After FY2027E revenue grows 10.0%, 8.0% and 6.0% as the Segafredo outlets open one at a time [S6 p.105], then fades to 4.0%.

**Margins.** The gross margin does not improve; it changes perimeter. FY2026E of 26.5% is the blend of a half year of fish at a low-teens margin and a half year of estate at the measured estate margin, which is the first-half actual rather than an assumption [S5 p.8, note 27]. From FY2027E the group prints 77.0%, because that is what the estate earned in the half year: food and beverage, rooms and other revenue against cost of revenue of a fraction of that revenue [S5 note 27]. We hold it flat. Nothing in the LK shows the estate margin deteriorating, and there is no recovery to the mid-forties group margin of FY2025A, which was the arithmetic of a different business. The step between FY2026E and FY2027E is the mix leaving, and a reader who wants to challenge the valuation should challenge the revenue path and the investment credit, not this line.

**Costs, depreciation and the stranded base.** The company reports depreciation inside operating expenses, at IDR10.5bn in FY2025A and IDR5.3bn in the first half of 2026 [S4, S5]. That matters twice over. It means the data pack depreciation is not the charge the profit and loss bears, so we restate it from the filing for FY2025A and FY2024A; and it means the single opex line in our model carries both cash cost and a nearly fixed depreciation charge. The charge did not leave with the trading book: the assets that left were construction in progress and inventory, not the depreciating property, so the estate now carries a charge sized for the group it used to be [S5 note 14]. That is why the opex ratio is 25.3% in the transition year and 85.7% in the first full estate year, falling to 68.9% by FY2030E and 66.0% at the end of the forecast only because revenue grows over a cost base that grows at about the rate of inflation. EBITDA margin lands at 18.8% in FY2026E, a blend of two perimeters, and 57.5% in FY2027E; EBIT is IDR-1.4bn in that year, below zero, because the estate keeps IDR12.2bn of gross profit before IDR10.5bn of depreciation and the residue is smaller than the cash operating cost it has to carry. That is the core financial fact of this file: the group kept the property and gave away the business that paid for it.

**How the estate's cash cost is allocated, and the range.** The filing does not split operating expense by segment. [S5 note 27] gives revenue and cost of revenue for the fish trade, food and beverage, rooms and other; [S5 note 30] gives general and administrative expense by nature, IDR8.3bn for the half year of which IDR5.3bn is depreciation. We therefore allocate the group's first-half cash cost equally between the two perimeters, which is close to their split of gross profit in that half: fish revenue of IDR45.1bn against cost of IDR40.3bn, and the estate's revenue of IDR52.5bn less the fish line against its much smaller cost of revenue [S5 note 27]. That half-share is the IDR13.6bn of FY2027E operating expense less IDR10.5bn of depreciation, and it is the largest single judgement in the operating forecast after the revenue path. The range is wide in both directions. A revenue-weighted allocation would put most of the overhead on the trading book that has left and leave the estate almost none, which is not credible for a banqueting venue, a hotel and a restaurant; a full carry would charge the estate for the trading desk as well and would put FY2027E EBIT lower by roughly the whole of the cash cost again. The full carry lowers the discounted cash flow and does not change the rating, because the operating business is already worth a small fraction of the equity value.

**Cash flow and the earnings-quality flags.** This is the centre of the earnings-quality review, and it is worth being precise about which flag fires. Reported net profit was IDR2.1bn in FY2025A while operating cash flow was IDR-1.3bn, and the same divergence appears in FY2024A, with profit of IDR3.1bn and operating cash flow of IDR-1.0bn, and in the pack earlier years [S4, S0]. The house card accruals ratio, however, is not the flag: profit less cash flow over average total assets is under one per cent of a total asset base of IDR369.0bn, well inside the ten per cent band the card sets [S4 p.9, S4 p.13]. What the card does flag is the absolute cash-conversion record, four consecutive years of negative operating cash flow against positive reported profit, and the divergence metrics: inventory of IDR69.5bn against inventories recognised as a cost of IDR22.5bn in the same year is well over a thousand days of stock [S4 note 7], receivables are not the issue at this scale, and the gap has not reversed. The asset that carried it has since left the operating book.

**The 30 June 2026 transfer: what the filing shows and what it does not.** Three facts, in order of weight. First, the arithmetic: inventory fell from IDR69.5bn to IDR8.6bn, fixed assets fell to IDR189.0bn, and other assets fell by a similar order; the falls sum to the new investment line of IDR162.5bn [S5 note 14, note 1d]. An investment that equals the operating net assets removed is the signature of a loss of control, not of a purchase. Second, the cash-flow statement: operating cash flow was slightly negative and investing cash flow nil, so no consideration was received and the transaction was a contribution, not a sale [S5 p.11]. Third, the classification: the stake sits in equity instruments at fair value through other comprehensive income [S5 note 3], which is the treatment of an interest the group does not control. Against that, the group structure note still lists PT Indo Nation Harvest among the consolidated subsidiaries at 30 June 2026 [S5 note 1d], but that table carries the same total asset figures as the previous year audited table for all three entities, down to the last thousand rupiah, with only the column headings changed [S4, S5 note 1d, F46]. A table that has not changed while the balance sheet around it moved by the size of the investment is a stale copy, and we do not treat it as evidence of continued control. The filing is internally inconsistent on this point; the dynamic evidence, the arithmetic and the classification all point the same way, and the base case follows them: the fish book leaves the consolidation from 1 July 2026. The disclosure does not settle what the group now owns, which is why the investment is carried at a discount and why the FY2026 audit is the event that matters.

**The working-capital correction.** The engine derives forecast working capital from a ratio to revenue, and the perimeter break creates two apparent releases inside free cash flow: one in FY2026E, when forecast working capital drops from the FY2025A operating balance of IDR63.7bn to a fraction of it, and one in FY2027E, when revenue steps down to the estate base. Neither is cash. The first is the inventory and receivables that left the operating book into the investment line; the second is the same disappearance one year later, because the trading book working capital went at the transfer, not in the forecast year [S5 note 14, S5 p.11]. The valuation reverses both in the bridge, so no phantom cash reaches the equity value. The DCF printed first-year free cash flow is therefore not the cash the business generates, and the report says so rather than leaving the reader to find it.

**Balance sheet and debt.** Equity was IDR342.6bn at the end of 2025 [S4]. Cash was IDR1.5bn at 31 December 2025 and IDR3.5bn at 30 June 2026; the bank loan was IDR17.5bn and the lease liability is little changed, so net debt at the half year is lower than the year-end figure the data pack carries [S4, S5]. The valuation dates the net debt to the half year for that reason. There is no dividend in the pack history [S0, S4], so capital allocation is entirely reinvestment, and the reinvestment has been a working-capital sink and an expansion of non-operating assets rather than capex in the operating estate.

**Capex.** Reported cash capex was effectively nil in FY2024A, FY2025A and the first half of 2026 [S4, S5], against gross property, plant and equipment several times the annual depreciation charge [S4]. Nil capex on a depreciating estate is not a maintenance rate; it is deferred spending. We model 3.0% of revenue in the transition year, rising to 53.0% and then held at the D&A ratio, so that the steady state replaces what it depreciates rather than running a perpetuity on capex below depreciation. The ratio is high only because the revenue denominator lost the trading book; in absolute rupiah the company spends more on maintenance each year of the forecast. Owner earnings, defined properly, are therefore lower than free cash flow in the early years, and close to the accounting charge at the end.

**Forecast summary.** Revenue IDR59.8bn in the transition year, IDR20.0bn five years out and IDR24.3bn at the end of the explicit forecast; EBIT IDR0.7bn to IDR2.6bn; net profit IDR-0.8bn to IDR2.6bn on 8,066 million shares, with return on equity still only 0.5% five years out and 0.7% in FY2035E, the final forecast year. A business that earns a low single-digit return on a large equity base ten years out is not compounding; it is subsisting, and the investment line is what the equity actually is [S5].

**Why this method set, and why one method.** The discounted cash flow is the only weighted method, at 100.0% of the value. That is a decision about this company rather than a taste: free cash flow is the only thing the filings let us measure with confidence, since the profit line is small enough that a single tax or related-party item moves it by half and the effective tax rate has already swung from above statutory to nil inside two years [S4, S5], and it is the only method whose perimeter matches the company after 30 June 2026. The market and peer multiples are discussed below as unweighted cross-checks, and they are not weighted for a mechanical reason worth stating plainly. The engine's multiple leg would apply a peer multiple to the pack's trailing FY2025A EBITDA, which still contains the fish book that left the consolidation, while the credit that replaces that book is added to the same equity value: that mixes two perimeters in a single number. Worse, the leg would share the same bridge, and two of those bridge items are the working-capital reversals that exist only inside the DCF's forecast because the perimeter break books a release that never arrived as cash. A trailing-EBITDA enterprise value contains no such release, so weighting the leg would debit it for cash it never received. We would rather publish one number we can build than two we cannot reconcile. P/E is not used even as a cross-check, because the profit base is under a per cent of revenue and the effective tax rate is unstable; P/BV is not used as a weighted method because the shares already trade at 1.7x book on a return on equity of 0.6%, and book value is a ceiling here rather than a valuation.
**Cost of capital.**

Risk-free at 7.4%, mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, country risk premium 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 0.90 raised above the industry default for a micro-cap with a violent price history and relevered to 0.92, giving a cost of equity of 12.0% and a WACC of 11.9% [S0]. That sits inside the house band for rupiah assets, so we do not argue it. Hold on to the comparison instead: a 12.0% cost of equity against a 0.6% return on equity means the company destroys value on every rupiah of retained earnings, and growth at a static margin makes the destruction larger rather than smaller.
**The discounted cash flow.**

The DCF produces Rp12 per share on an enterprise value of IDR90.3bn, with the terminal value only 6.9% of that. The low terminal share is not a forecasting flourish: the first forecast year still prints a large working-capital release that never became cash, which is reversed in the bridge below, and the terminal year spends what it depreciates, so the perpetuity adds little on top of a ten-year stream. A reader who thinks the terminal share should be higher is really saying that capex should be below depreciation forever; that is a value assumption, not a forecast, and it is not in this model. The DCF own first-year free cash flow, net of the reversal, is a fraction of the line printed.

**The bridge, and the investment credit as a house judgement.** The IDR162.5bn investment is the one asset the price rests on and the filings do not explain. The bridge carries it in four legs, as one transaction, and the first leg has two separate adjustments on it. The valuation haircut is thirty per cent: the source supports the book value only, so the discount for undisclosed ownership and earnings, the inventory the auditor made a key audit matter for existence and valuation, and the absence of any impairment test is our judgement, not a measured number [S5 note 14, S4]. On top of the haircut, and separate from it, the line carries a twenty-five per cent probability of a total write-down, which is the medium-likelihood, high-impact risk in the next section expressed as a number and applied in every scenario rather than only in the bear. The two multiply: the expected value of the line is just over half of book. Against the credit sit two reversals of the working-capital releases described in the financial section, and one addition: net debt dated to 30 June 2026, the date of the investment, because the data pack still carries 31 December 2025 cash. Net, the bridge leaves the expected credit less the two reversals and plus the net-debt dating, and that net figure is a small part of the gap between the IDR580.7bn the market pays and the equity value we publish; the operating business falling short of the price does the rest.

Because both adjustments are ours, the file carries the sensitivity rather than assuming it away. Set the write-down probability aside and value the line at seven-tenths of book and the equity value rises by the quarter of the credit the probability withholds; add the haircut back too, and value it at full book, and the value rises by the rest of the line — the asset case, and still far below Rp72. Set the credit to zero, which is the write-down actually happening, and the equity value falls by the whole of the net bridge and what remains is the estate's own cash flows after the two reversals and the dated net debt, a small fraction of what we publish. What would move either adjustment: the ownership percentages and any share of profit for the three investees; a fair-value exercise or a transaction price; an impairment test, or its absence, in the FY2026 audit; and any distribution received from the entities. Until one of those appears, the credit stays a judgement and the sensitivity stays in the report.
**The cross-checks, and why they are not weighted.**

Three unweighted checks, all pointing the same way. First, the market's own multiple: the shares trade at 40.1x trailing EV/EBITDA on an EBITDA that still contains the fish book, against the single-digit trailing multiples of the closest listed comparables, SKBM, CAMP and CEKA [S0]. Applying a peer multiple to that trailing EBITDA is the calculation we declined above, because the engine would carry it through the same bridge as the DCF and debit it for the working-capital reversals that only exist in the DCF's forecast — the divergence that calculation produces is an artefact of the shared bridge, not an opinion about the business. Second, book: book value per share is Rp42 against a price of Rp72, so the market already pays a premium to a balance sheet that carries the investment line at full book and the property at cost. Third, the exit: the terminal value is only 6.9% of enterprise value and it implies an exit below the entry the DCF pays, set out in the next paragraph. The chain itself is short and there is no second opinion inside it: the method value is Rp12, the probability-weighted scenario target Rp16 before the liquidity discount, and the published target Rp14 — three steps of one model, run once.

**Reinvestment, return on incremental capital and the exit test.** The compounder frame is the right test for this file because the whole question is whether retained cash earns a return. It does not, and the arithmetic is in the model rather than in adjectives: capex is carried at 53.0% of revenue by FY2030E to replace a depreciation charge of IDR10.5bn, and the return on the equity that funds it is 0.5% five years out and 0.7% at the end of the forecast [S4, S5]. A reinvestment rate at that level of capex multiplied by that return is a growth rate below the terminal growth we allow, which is why the perpetuity is the least supported part of the value and the smallest. Every rupiah of operating cash flow has been retained and more, yet EBIT is IDR4.5bn on a total asset base of IDR369.0bn, a return on the operating asset base in low single digits and negative once the property is charged at its depreciation [S4, S5]. Incremental capital in the last two years went into working capital and then into the investment line, not into the estate that earns the revenue. On the exit test the card asks for: the terminal value is 6.9% of enterprise value, so the exit is barely tested, and against terminal EBITDA of IDR14.8bn and terminal EBIT of IDR2.6bn the exit implied by that terminal value is below the entry the DCF pays on IDR14.9bn of trailing EBITDA. There is no multiple expansion hidden in the terminal value; the perpetuity holds its value because the terminal cash flow is capitalised at the cost of capital, not because the business is sold well.

**What the investment line is worth, and why it does not rescue the price.** Book value per share is Rp42 and the shares trade at Rp72, so the market pays a premium to a balance sheet that includes IDR162.5bn of investments and a property estate carried at cost. Take the asset case at face value and it still fails on its own terms: it requires that the investments are worth book, that the related-party receivable of IDR3.5bn is recoverable, that the land held under a binding sale-and-purchase agreement with the seller name still on the title is worth its carrying value, and that the inventory the auditor made a key matter of is worth its carrying value [S5, S4]. Grant all four and the shares are worth book per share while trading at a multiple of it. At our haircut and write-down probability, and net of the working-capital corrections the transfer created, the investment covers only a small part of the gap between our value and the price. The asset case is not a bull case; it is a ceiling below the price unless the property itself is worth more than its cash generation supports, which the filings do not claim and no appraisal evidences.
**Sensitivity.**

Value is most sensitive to the revenue path and the gross margin, which is what a property-backed estate should look like, and least sensitive to the discount rate: a point either way on the WACC moves the DCF by a small amount, because the terminal value is a small share of the enterprise and the cash flows are close to flat in real terms. That insensitivity is worth saying plainly: whether the WACC should be a point higher does not change the conclusion. The sensitivity that does change the answer is the investment credit, and it is set out above.

**What the price implies.** The reverse DCF cannot bracket the price: even at the top of the growth range it tests, our model values the shares below Rp72. That is the cleanest statement of the variant view. At Rp72 the market capitalisation is IDR580.7bn against a target value of Rp14 a share, and the trailing multiple is 40.1x on EBITDA that still contains a business the group no longer consolidates. The market is not pricing the current perimeter at any growth rate the model will generate. It is pricing a franchise rollout at a scale and pace the company has not demonstrated, and an investment whose worth nobody has disclosed, on a capital base it does not have.

The base case is the most probable path, not the most cautious one: the transfer stands, the second half carries the estate at the level the first half actually printed, the measured estate margin holds, capex is brought to a maintenance rate and the stated rollout is credited one outlet at a time. The bear is the operating downside around that base, with revenue growth and margin shocked in mirror image to the bull. The bull reverses the transfer in substance: either the group structure note is right and the fish book is reconsolidated, or the investees pay a market rent for the property the group kept, so revenue grows faster than the base each year. The shocks are mirrored in both directions and the narratives match them.

Scenarios carry a base probability of 50.0%, with the bear at 25.0% and the bull at 25.0%. The base value is Rp13 a year out (Rp12 before the roll-forward at the cost of equity), the bear Rp11 and the bull Rp25. Three qualifications, because the table cannot carry them. First, the probability weights are ours, and the base carries half of it because the perimeter evidence points one way while one note in the filing contradicts it; a reader who weights the bull more heavily should know that even the bull value is a fraction of Rp72, so the direction of the call does not depend on the weights. Second, the write-down risk is not a fourth state and not a separate bear: it is priced into every state at once, as the twenty-five per cent probability of total loss carried on the credit in the bridge, which is why the base, the bear and the bull all sit below the values they would carry at the full credit. There is no second bear to print, because the write-down is in the first one and in the bull as well. Third, the bull moves the value much more than the bear does, and that is arithmetic rather than a lopsided shock set: the base's operating business is worth close to nothing after the working-capital reversals, so a mirrored improvement in growth, margin and cost is a large multiple of a small number, while the credit anchors the downside.
**Downside risks, with likelihood and impact.**

*The investment line is worth less than book, or nothing. Medium likelihood, high impact.* IDR162.5bn of assets with no disclosed earnings, created from inventory the auditor had questioned and from construction in progress that stopped being depreciated in the operating business, classified as equity instruments at fair value through other comprehensive income rather than as a controlled business [S5 note 3, S5 note 14]. A material impairment would remove the largest asset and the only thing supporting the equity value above the estate cash generation. This is the highest-impact single item in the file, and it is why the credit is a judgement with a stated range rather than a number: a twenty-five per cent chance of total loss is what "medium likelihood" means in this model, and it is charged against the line in every scenario in the table above.

*The estate cannot carry its property base. Medium likelihood, high impact.* The depreciation charge is sized for the group that existed before the transfer, and the revenue that used to cover it now sits in the investees [S5 note 14]. If banqueting and hotel volume does not grow into that base, EBIT stays negative, no dividend is possible, and the property becomes a disposal candidate at a price nobody has disclosed. This is the arithmetic the base already carries; the risk is that it is worse than the base because the Segafredo rollout slips.

*The perimeter reading is wrong and the fish book still consolidates. Medium likelihood, high impact, to the upside.* The group structure note still lists the fish entity as a subsidiary, and if the audit confirms it, the revenue we have removed belongs to the group and the forecast is too low [S5 note 1d]. We judge this the less likely reading because the table is a stale copy of the prior year table and the balance-sheet arithmetic points the other way, but it is a genuine open question and the FY2026 audit settles it. It is the reason the bull scenario exists.

*Governance and related-party gravity. Medium likelihood, medium impact.* A receivable of IDR3.5bn from the controlling shareholder, land held under an agreement with a shareholder name on the title, an investment in three entities whose ownership is not disclosed, and a filing that contradicts itself on whether one of them is a subsidiary [S5, S4]. On this exchange related-party flows are the modal value-destruction channel, and this company has the structure for it. The internal inconsistency in the half-year notes is itself a disclosure-quality flag.

*Liquidity and index mechanics. High likelihood, medium impact.* Average daily traded value of IDR1.3bn on a 36.0% float [S0]. Our target applies a discount for it. A holder cannot express a view here at scale, and the price can move on very little flow, which is visible in a range from Rp50 to Rp183 over a year [S0]. The FTSE Russell December 2026 quarterly review deletes several Indonesian micro caps from its global indices with effect from 21 December 2026; IBOS is not among the named deletions, so this is a read-across to the sector rather than a forced-supply event in the stock [S11].

*Franchise execution and capital. Medium likelihood, medium impact.* The Segafredo licence is real and exclusive and the first outlet is open [S9]. But the rollout needs capital the operating cash flow does not generate, in a business that has never paid a dividend [S4]. Dilution, or debt the filings do not currently show, is the likely funding route, and either would come at the expense of the equity value per share.

*Regulatory and food-safety. Low likelihood, high impact.* A halal, food-safety or import-quarantine event in the estate would hit the brand and the licence. Standard for the sector, not specific to this name.

**The bull case, stated honestly.** The bull is not absurd. An exclusive national franchise licence for an established Italian coffee brand, in a market where coffee chains have compounded, held by a company with an existing restaurant operation and a banqueting venue, is a plausible value-creation story. The bull also carries the possibility that the transfer is reversed in substance, with the fish book reconsolidated or the property let to the investees at a market rent, which would restore revenue the base has removed. Add the growth path, the outlets on schedule and the estate margin holding, and the shares are worth Rp25. That is still a fraction of Rp72: the market is paying for more than the bull, which is the point.

**Signposts that would change the view.** Disclosure of the ownership and earnings of the three investees; an FY2026 audit showing the fish book still consolidated and the investment line carrying real profit; a distribution from the investees or a market rent on the property; and a funded, dated outlet rollout with disclosed unit economics. A write-down of the investment line, or an FY2026 result with second-half revenue far below the first half, would confirm the base or the bear. The first two would move us up, and the third would move the value most, because it is the only one that would turn the investment from a judgement into a priced asset.

**Ownership and control.** Insiders hold 61.5% and the free float is 36.0%, with no institutional holder disclosed [S0]. PT Goldman Investindo Sedaya is the controlling vehicle and appears in the interim filing with a direct stake of just under half the register [S5]. The board comprises Nita Fredrika as president commissioner and Edi Nugroho as president director, alongside the commissioners and directors named in the annual report [S6]. A register this concentrated with a float this small leaves minority holders without a practical voice, and the float is small enough that index mechanics, not fundamentals, can dominate price moves.

**Disclosure quality.** The half-year notes contradict themselves on the most important transaction of the year. The investment note introduces IDR162.5bn of investments in three entities, and one of them is listed in the group structure note as a ninety-nine per cent-owned consolidated subsidiary, with total assets identical to the prior year audited figure for all three entities [S5 note 14, S5 note 1d, F46]. Two notes in the same filing cannot both describe the group. We treat the table as stale because its figures did not move while the balance sheet around it did, but the inconsistency is a disclosure flag in its own right, and it sits on the balance-sheet item that carries most of the equity value.

**Related-party flows.** Three items, in ascending order of concern, and the method card asks for them quantified rather than listed. A receivable of IDR3.5bn at 30 June 2026: [S5 note 7] names the counterparty as PT Goldman Investindo Sedaya, the controlling shareholder, describes a loan made under an April 2025 agreement at two per cent a year, and records the company's own explanation that it was made in the context of a reciprocal business relationship in which the shareholder provides business and marketing networks. Against the balance sheet that is a small exposure — IDR369.0bn of total assets and IDR42.8bn of FY2025 revenue [S4] — but against the estate's cash generation it is not, because the loan is several times the group's FY2025 operating cash flow of IDR-1.3bn [S4]. Land and a warehouse in Surabaya held as investment property under a sale-and-purchase binding agreement dated 12 May 2020 with a party the note itself describes as a shareholder, with the title still in that party name [S4]: the company occupies and books the asset but does not own the legal title. And the investment line of IDR162.5bn in three entities whose ownership percentages and earnings are not disclosed, classified as equity instruments at fair value through other comprehensive income [S5 note 3, S5 note 14], which is the largest single related-party-adjacent exposure in the file and the one the valuation haircut is charged against. None of this is evidence of misappropriation. Together it is the structure through which value can move without a minority holder seeing it, which is why the method card treats related-party gravity as the modal risk on this exchange.

**Auditor and opinion.** The audit is signed by a small local registered public accounting firm, with an unqualified opinion and a single key audit matter: the valuation and existence of inventories [S4]. That key matter is the flag that matters. The auditor own words say the risk is that inventory does not exist or is not valued in line with the accounting policy, and no provision was taken in that year [S4]. A year later that inventory was largely converted into the investment line, and no impairment test on the resulting balance is disclosed [S5]. We do not allege a problem we can prove. We say the audit trail runs out exactly where the largest asset on the balance sheet begins.

**Capital allocation and dividend record.** No dividend in the pack history and none proposed [S0, S4]. With negative operating cash flow and a rollout to fund, that is at least coherent. It also means the return to a minority holder depends entirely on a re-rating, in a stock that has already moved between Rp183 and Rp50 inside a year [S0].

**Other structure flags.** No special-monitoring board status or notation letter appears in the documents we archived [S4, S5], and the share count of 8,066 million did not change between December and June [S5]. We found no rights issue, pledged-share disclosure or auditor down-tier in the filings read for this note. The transfer itself was disclosed only through the balance sheet and the notes, with no announcement we could find in the company own disclosures.

**ESG.** The material exposures are ordinary for the sector and largely unmanaged at this scale: food safety and cold-chain integrity in the estate, halal and hygiene certification, labour standards in a business with 38 direct employees and an undisclosed contracted workforce, and packaging waste in the canned drink line [S6]. Governance is the dominant factor here rather than environmental or social metrics, and the specific weaknesses are the disclosure contradiction and the related-party items above.

**Dated catalysts.** The FY2026 audited accounts are the event that matters, expected by the end of the first quarter of 2027 on the usual exchange timetable [S4]. That filing answers the two questions this note cannot: whether the fish-trading book is still consolidated at the revenue level we have removed, and whether the IDR162.5bn investment line carries earnings. Before that, any announcement on the three investees, or an impairment, is the news risk [S5]. The FTSE Russell December 2026 review takes effect on 21 December 2026 and does not name IBOS, so the forced-supply date that matters for several micro-cap peers does not apply here; a later review that does would be a dated supply event [S11]. The Segafredo rollout is the running catalyst: the Yogyakarta flagship opened in early November 2026, and each additional outlet, with the airport terminals named in the annual report the obvious next ones, is evidence for or against the bull case [S9, S6].

**KPIs we monitor.** The investment line first: any change in its balance, any equity-accounted income, any impairment note, and above all the ownership percentages of the three investees, because that one disclosure would replace the judgement in our valuation with a number [S5]. The estate revenue and gross margin by segment, because they now decide the equity [S5]. Operating cash flow against reported profit every period, because that divergence is the earnings-quality flag that has persisted longest [S4]. The depreciation charge relative to revenue, because it measures whether the retained property base is being carried or supported [S4, S5]. Capex, because the forecast assumes the estate is brought back to a maintenance rate and a third year of nil spend would falsify it [S4]. Working-capital turnover on the estate perimeter, not on the old group. And the rollover of the bank loan of IDR17.5bn with no disclosed facility headroom [S5].

**What would make us wrong on the upside.** A disclosed, audited, profitable investment balance would add value our model carries only at a discount; a market rent on the property would turn the stranded cost base into a revenue line; and a fast, well-funded franchise rollout with visible unit economics would change the growth path rather than the margin. None is in the filings today. If any arrives the target moves and we will say so; the price today already assumes all three [S5, S9].
